sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Aaron Swift's bronze-tier case is the cleanest street workflow on record, the 'blocking and tackling' files that keep the lights on. Intake filters each consumer into litigation, disputes, or a credit-repair affiliate partner, then the firm sends third-party collectors a letter by fax or email [owpVxkqEbEk @ 00:03:10]. Swift stresses it is not a validation letter, which only matters inside the first 30 days; it is built on Reg F, restricts contact channels and times such as 5:00 to 8:00 p.m., and disputes the debt. The trap then springs on its own. The collector kept texting, and the credit reports never marked the account disputed. Loman confirms the second hook: when a collector tradeline such as LVNV or Portfolio Recovery is disputed, it must be marked disputed [n3SZjPQDSHc @ 00:14:16]. Swift's payout on those two technical violations: about $4,000 of debt forgiven, the tradeline deleted, $1,000 in statutory damages, roughly $4,500 in attorney fees, and about $450 to the affiliate as contract paralegal [owpVxkqEbEk @ 00:05:22]. Swift calls the result a debt almost completely erased like it never existed. The unit economics are the point. A low-dollar file with a fax letter and two missed obligations funds the attorney, the affiliate, and a near-total debt wipe for the client.

Once a file goes to suit, John Watts lays out the procedural rhythm. He files in state court 99.9 percent of the time because of Spokeo standing arguments, and defendants, who get 30 days to answer or remove, remove 99.9 percent of the time [Ce0D7z4zJFo @ 00:00:30]. Motions to dismiss are often baseless because 'it makes the lawyers money,' so he usually amends the complaint as of right instead. Discovery then runs through interrogatories, document requests, requests for admission, and depositions, followed by summary judgment with damages usually left to the jury [Ce0D7z4zJFo @ 00:03:32]. At trial he calls the collector's own witnesses, and the collector's motion for judgment as a matter of law has always been denied in his trials. Swift tempers the trial math: the vast majority, 99 percent or more, never reach trial [owpVxkqEbEk @ 00:01:14]. Brian Parker shows what discovery can surface on the other side. Deposing collection attorney Bradley Johnson, he extracted that the firm files about 50 suits a week, roughly 10 a day, off a form complaint with an auto-generated summons, scrubbing through LexisNexis for deceased, new addresses, bankruptcy, and active military [RwXTJhX-rxo @ 00:21:52]. Volume filing on templates is exactly what deposition questioning is built to expose.

The balance itself is the next attack surface. Loman's hospital-debt workflow starts with a HIPAA request for medical records including billing, because the collector is not required to itemize under 'G' of the FDCPA, then pulls an insurance accounting of what was paid; he routinely finds double billing and code changes [n3SZjPQDSHc @ 00:41:14]. Host Hannah Locklear was charged $16 for one ibuprofen pill and got the debt lowered after demanding an itemized statement, and Loman has a client billed $6,000 for a $300 IV. Brian Parker hunts the same inflation through §1692f: every charge must sit inside the four corners of the contract, and an unauthorized 25% collection fee is a violation [YYdsx06msa0 @ 00:03:38]. He also stacks claims, since false credit reporting under §1692e8 supports an FCRA claim too, so 'you can hit them twice' [YYdsx06msa0 @ 00:01:13]. Parker frames these as strict-liability violations. None of this works without proof of delivery. Jermaine, drawing on his time working in debt collections, insists on copying every letter and sending it certified, not regular mail or email, for a 16-digit tracking number, because otherwise it is your word against the collector's [XSfDS_s1URg @ 00:06:09]. Many collectors, he warns, never fix errors after being called out, so the documented file is the weapon.

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split on call frequency is whether seven attempts in seven days is a wall or a tripwire. Kaiser Jansen, appearing on SeniorLiving.Org, frames it as absolute: "now debt collectors can only attempt to call you seven times in seven days that's it," and adds that the count runs per account, so a consumer carrying five accounts can absorb up to 35 calls in a week [9RtU4rpS3pw @ 00:05:51]. Night Ferry reads the same rule as a presumption of violation rather than a hard cap, and notes that texts and emails are not counted toward it, though each must still offer a simple opt-out [7HVra7o-cZg @ 00:03:24]. Jeff Loman of Guardian Litigation Group pushes the frequency fight further, citing case law where 18 calls in a single day were not treated as harassing unless the collector actually spoke with the consumer [n3SZjPQDSHc @ 00:08:09]. Michael Stillman, past president of the NCBA, attacks the rule from the collection-bar side: after a right-party contact, no further contact is allowed within seven days without consent, which collides head-on with judges who order a hallway call, prompting the attorney to ask the bench, "are you also going to indemnify me" [9VNthZZ6JNk @ 00:08:37].

Practitioners also split on how dangerous a single payment is on old paper. Jansen tells SeniorLiving.Org viewers that a payment resets the statute of limitations in "almost every state," naming Texas as the exception, and pairs that with the ban on threatening suit over time-barred debt [9RtU4rpS3pw @ 00:17:58]. WealthCurve opens with a narrower warning that paying can restart the clock only "in some states," puts typical limitation periods at three to six years, and points to a 2023 CFPB advisory barring suit threats on time-barred debt [cKYmFnf_o2Q @ 00:04:42]. Loman widens the trigger list beyond money: a payment, a payment plan, or even an admission can reset the clock, and the statute only limits lawsuits, so collection can continue "forever" while credit reporting runs seven years [n3SZjPQDSHc @ 00:29:22]. Brian Parker of KillDebt takes the most aggressive posture on threatened suits under section 1692e5, telling consumers to "wait it out" when a collector threatens litigation, and stressing that nobody can be garnished without a judgment [YYdsx06msa0 @ 00:07:04]. The playbook choice is stark: Jansen and Loman treat any engagement on stale debt as a reset risk, while Parker treats an empty threat of suit as a strict-liability violation in its own right.

The paperwork camp splits hardest on how much to demand from a collector. Meet Jermaine, drawing on time spent working in debt collections, hands out a free four-letter bundle covering pay to delete, goodwill, cease and desist, and debt validation [XSfDS_s1URg @ 00:00:19]. Loman flatly rejects the 28-item validation demands circulating online: "That is absolutely not the law," explaining that only three items are required, and warning that a written pay-for-delete can get an attorney classed as a credit repair organization, so the safer route is getting deletion by email or informally [n3SZjPQDSHc @ 00:34:56]. Attorney Aaron Swift runs a third playbook, sending third-party collectors a letter by fax or email that is explicitly not a validation letter, because validation only matters inside the first 30 days; it is built on Reg F, restricts contact channels and times such as 5:00 to 8:00 p.m., and disputes the debt [owpVxkqEbEk @ 00:03:29]. Jermaine insists every letter go by certified mail for a 16-digit tracking number, because with regular mail it is "your word against" the collector's, while Swift reports that his letter, followed by two technical violations, wiped roughly $4,000 of debt for a bronze-tier client.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The cheapest losses are self-inflicted on the phone and at the mailbox. Jansen warns that simply saying "okay" when a collector asks to call back counts as consent, which quietly unlocks contact the seven-in-seven rule would otherwise block [9RtU4rpS3pw @ 00:06:29]. WealthCurve flags two timing traps: the dispute must be in writing and should not be mailed on day 29 of the 30-day window, and the one-year limit to sue runs from the violation, not from when the consumer discovers it [cKYmFnf_o2Q @ 00:07:18]. Night Ferry puts the scale of the biggest trap on the table, citing Pew 2020 data that more than 70% of collection suits end in default judgments, and noting garnishment is capped at 25% with weekly income of $217.50 or less exempt [7HVra7o-cZg @ 00:06:18]. Loman is blunt about ignoring a lawsuit: never do it, because bank accounts can be levied and frozen years later, defenses are gone once judgment is entered, and there is no statute of limitations on a stipulated judgment; vacating one is a state-court fight that would need a $5,000 to $10,000 retainer [n3SZjPQDSHc @ 00:32:24]. Loman also reports that Arizona judgments last ten years, are renewable, and can reach four times the original amount.

Consumers who do sue hit their own walls. Meet Jermaine walks through a Southern District of Ohio case against Portfolio Recovery Associates where the plaintiff alleged inaccurate disputed-status reporting and collection without verification, and the court granted summary judgment for PRA because it followed reasonable procedures and the errors were unintentional [XSfDS_s1URg @ 00:02:59]. LawShelf identifies that same bona fide error defense, along with good-faith reliance on an FTC advisory opinion, as the main escape hatches for collectors [i6PAssklgJg @ 00:06:40]. Watts adds a structural trap that catches debtors who think a violation erases the balance: a section 1692g violation is not a defense against the debt, only a claim against the collector [qTSer3pu6io @ 01:01:14]. Loman tempers damages expectations, putting statutory damages at $100 to $1,000 and reporting that some clients have received $1, while warning that non-lump-sum settlements get filed with the court, so a single missed payment produces an immediate judgment, and roughly 30% of litigated files fail to update to Metro 2 code 64 with a zero balance afterward [n3SZjPQDSHc @ 00:25:48]. The lesson from Jermaine is operational: copy every letter and keep documentation, because many collectors do not fix errors even after being called out.

On the other side of the table, the economics run on volume, and volume breaks. Brian Parker's deposition of collection attorney Bradley Johnson extracted the admission "we do about 50 a week so 10 a day," with the complaint built from a form, the summons auto-generated, and address scrubbing outsourced to LexisNexis with no state-ID search [RwXTJhX-rxo @ 00:21:52]. The same deposition exposed a December 2022 affidavit that called Security Credit Services "plaintiff" before any suit existed, never attached its Exhibit A, and carried no penalty-of-perjury clause, prompting Parker's line that "an affidavit is not an affidavit unless it's signed under penalty of perjury"; Colin Ward still paid $2,500 in settlement [RwXTJhX-rxo @ 01:53:36]. Swift's silver case shows stubbornness turning into losses: Discover lost one suit, then sued again seven years later through a new collector using the same lawyers, and the consumer counterclaimed for over $50,000 [owpVxkqEbEk @ 00:08:31]. Watts lays out why buyers keep pushing: Crown "buys a thousand dollar debt for fifty bucks" and a consumer may settle for $700, yet the court held that hiring a third party to collect does not let a principal-purpose buyer escape the FDCPA [fPw38bPWFtw @ 00:03:48].

callout.title: Four checks before engaging any collector
callout.body: Each check is drawn from losses, reversals, or traps the practitioners reported firsthand.
items: Send the written dispute early by certified mail with return receipt; never mail it on day 29 of the 30-day window [WealthCurve — cKYmFnf_o2Q @ 00:03:01].
Do not answer okay to a collector's request to call back unless further contact is intended, because it counts as consent [SeniorLiving.Org — 9RtU4rpS3pw @ 00:06:29].
Never ignore a filed collection suit; once judgment is entered the defenses are gone and accounts can be levied years later [Solo – Resolve Your Debt — n3SZjPQDSHc @ 00:32:24].

Build the evidence file before suing: a copy of every letter and its 16-digit certified tracking number, since PRA beat a reporting claim on bona fide error [Meet Jermaine (Clear &Strategic) — XSfDS_s1URg @ 00:06:09].

chapters.question_prompt: How long do judgments and debts stay collectible, and what defenses and resistance tactics do debtors use against collection?
chapters.title: Judgment Lifespan, Statutes of Limitation, and Debtor Resistance
chapters.subtitle: Judgment duration and revival, statutes of limitation on debts and judgments, the IRS 10-year collection statute and tolling, winning or defending debt-collection lawsuits, testimony mistakes, summary judgment, asset-protection strategies to avoid paying, and sovereign-citizen defiance ending in contempt
chapters.executive_summary: Judgment-recovery and debt-defense operators agree that judgments outlive the debts behind them. The Business Guy puts typical lifespans at 10 to 20 years, and renewable states like Oklahoma allow indefinite five-year renewals. Weston Legal and Steve Richardson stress that once a suit is filed, the statute of limitations stops running. Stephen A Williams documents collectors buying dormant judgments and reviving them, often past state revival deadlines that unrepresented debtors never check. On defense, John Skiba reports that 95% of sued consumers default. Skiba turns AAA arbitration economics, roughly $200 for the consumer versus $2,500 to $5,000 for the creditor, into dismissals. Former IRS agent Mike Sullivan and Bob Jablonsky map the IRS 10-year collection clock and its tolling events. The split is over posture: offshore trusts and asset shielding versus answering, arbitrating, settling, or filing bankruptcy.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus: Judgments Outlive the Debt, and the Clock Only Helps People Who Track It
paragraphs: Across the asset-protection, credit-repair, and consumer-defense camps, operators agree on one baseline fact: a judgment is a far longer-lived weapon than the underlying debt. The Business Guy of Asset Protection Planners puts the general lifespan at 10 to 20 years, with some states letting judgments run for the rest of the debtor's life [nbtlIEi4we0 @ 00:00:00]. Their state examples are blunt. California runs 10 years, renewable for another 10. Oklahoma expires in five years but lets the creditor renew every five years indefinitely, and each renewal restarts the clock [nbtlIEi4we0 @ 00:02:28]. Weston Legal draws the same contrast from the lawsuit side: creditors typically get 4, 5, or 6 years to sue, but a judgment they win can last 20 years in many states [HD3idZhyATA @ 00:00:48]. Stephen A Williams of The Credit Repair Shop frames the outer wall as a 20-year maximum on civil judgments, outside student loans. Inside that window, each state has a dormancy mechanism that kills renewal if the holder sleeps past its date [--FOsBTlu2E @ 00:03:32]. The takeaway is consistent: an old debt and a dead judgment are different animals. The date that matters is the renewal or revival deadline in the specific state.

The second point of agreement kills a popular street myth: dodging the process server or waiting out the calendar after a suit is filed does nothing. Steve Richardson, a collection defense attorney in southern New Jersey, says a question they field constantly comes from people whose bank accounts are being levied on a 10-year-old judgment. The answer: once suit is brought, and especially once judgment is entered, the statute of limitations no longer applies [wibZgw9EKZ4 @ 00:00:27]. Richardson's New Jersey numbers for the pre-suit window are four years for sale of goods and six years for services and credit card balances, running from charge-off [wibZgw9EKZ4 @ 00:01:25]. Weston Legal hits the service angle directly. People try to avoid the process server until the limitations period runs, but the clock stops when the lawsuit is filed, not when the defendant is served [HD3idZhyATA @ 00:00:34]. John Skiba of Consumer Warrior supplies the flip side, the one window where the limitations clock is a live weapon. If the creditor filed after expiration, such as past Arizona's six-year credit card period, the defendant can move to dismiss [7TbwIGMYgYE @ 00:02:26]. Timing defenses live before filing; after judgment, the fight moves to enforcement, renewal, and assets.

The third consensus is that the debtor who disengages hands the creditor the win. Skiba reports that about 95% of people sued by a debt collector never file an answer. Without an answer the game is over: judgment, then wage garnishment or a bank levy [fWHpyqQu_5M @ 00:01:13]. The Business Guy adds a mechanical nuance that cuts both ways. A judgment does not force the debtor to start paying; the creditor has to act under state law to seize assets. Failure to pay is not punishable by contempt or jail, outside exceptions like child or spousal support [5mmy9Xz_Oko @ 00:00:58]. That passivity is exactly what revivers exploit. Williams warns that when the debtor does not show up, collectors buying old judgments push renewals through uncontested and extend collection out to the full 20 years [4Mctc4AuqWA @ 00:10:05]. Courtroom footage from verdict sentencestv shows the opposite failure: sovereign-style refusal. A tenant told an Austin, Texas justice court "we don't accept or consent." The judge answered that the order stands whether they consent or not, that it becomes final, and that it supports a writ of possession [HPD6TM130zk @ 00:10:38]. Show up, answer, and fight on the rules, not around them.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers: Revival Audits, Arbitration Economics, and the IRS Clock
paragraphs: The sharpest street mechanic on the judgment side is the revival audit. Williams describes a booming business: collectors canvass the country for uncollected judgments, then buy them from the original creditor or another collector, or offer to collect by reviving them [4Mctc4AuqWA @ 00:00:19]. The buyer files the forms, pays any local court fee, and requests a hearing date to have the judgment revived [--FOsBTlu2E @ 00:02:37]. Williams' state-by-state revival read-through gives the deadlines to check first: Alabama 10 years, with revival required inside that 10; Florida a flat 20; Illinois seven; Kentucky 15; and Texas, startlingly, within two years [4Mctc4AuqWA @ 00:02:31]. The payoff comes when the dates do not line up. One Ohio caller faced a revival that Williams' team found sat under a 10-year revival window but was filed 12 years out, two years past the deadline. Williams says these collectors simply do not expect people to know [--FOsBTlu2E @ 00:04:17]. Williams read the list live and flagged Florida and New Hampshire for a re-check, so the figures are a starting map, not a final one. The workflow: pull the revival petition, match it to the state window, and appear to contest anything filed late.

In the lawsuit phase, Skiba's highest-leverage move is forcing the case out of court and into private arbitration. The mechanics: answer the suit, get the card agreement, find the arbitration clause, and file a motion asking the court to move the case [fWHpyqQu_5M @ 00:05:34]. If the creditor has not produced the terms, Skiba points to the CFPB website's database of almost every credit card agreement ever issued, downloadable free [fWHpyqQu_5M @ 00:09:28]. The motion to compel attaches the clause and tells the judge that either party can request arbitration [7TbwIGMYgYE @ 00:05:27]. Skiba says creditors almost never invoke the clause themselves, because their model is a cheap judgment followed by garnishment. The economics are the weapon. The consumer's AAA filing fee runs about $200, while the creditor must front $2,500 to $5,000 depending on case size. That makes chasing a $3,500 claim pointless, so creditors usually dismiss or agree to a mutual walk-away [fWHpyqQu_5M @ 00:07:45]. Skiba's one condition is good faith: actually file with AAA, pay the fee, and be ready to proceed. If the creditor refuses to pay its share, AAA closes the case and the court will often dismiss. Arbitration rules are also relaxed enough for self-represented defendants; Skiba once faced an arbitrator in jeans and a T-shirt on Zoom.

For tax debt the clock is federal and mechanical. Mike Sullivan, a former IRS agent, puts the collection statute at 10 years from the date of assessment. The IRS logs that as the 23C or TC 150 date, generally within six weeks of filing [go3rRhIEajA @ 00:00:56]. Bob Jablonsky, an enrolled agent in Richardson, Texas, says e-filed returns are typically assessed on the filing date. Paper returns and IRS substitute-for-return filings start the clock once processed [KU5hNE5Z2MU @ 00:01:21]. Tolling events stack on top. Sullivan lists an offer in compromise (a year plus its pending time), bankruptcy (the time spent in it), a taxpayer assistance order, and collection due process hearings that usually run three to five months. Long offers or bankruptcies can push the total to 12 years [0jHEJqFcgLA @ 00:01:41]. Jablonsky adds that bankruptcy tolls for its duration plus six months. Their tactical rule is to run the math before filing anything. At nine years and ten months past assessment, an offer only extends the clock, so letting the statute expire can be the smarter play. Repeated offers that will never be accepted just hand the IRS more time [KU5hNE5Z2MU @ 00:04:54]. At expiry, Sullivan says filed federal tax liens self-release.

callout.title: Field Tricks the Collectors Count on You Missing
callout.body: Four moves practitioners use to read the collector's playbook and avoid handing them the case.
items: Never agree that you owe the debt buyer's client. A bill of sale is only part of the purchase and sale agreement, so you need the whole document to know what was bought; answer "I do not know" unless you have personal knowledge [Alabama Consumer Protection Lawyers — xF2ZuR2-O4o @ 00:05:45]

Lawsuits that land all at once are often coordinated. Credit bureaus sell trigger reports that flag changes like buying a car or house, signaling to creditors that you may be collectible again [Consumer Warrior — fWHpyqQu_5M @ 00:11:57]

Collectors skip-trace through credit reports to see car and mortgage payments. One debtor found them photographing her cars and house before enforcing a judgment [The Credit Repair Shop — --FOsBTlu2E @ 00:07:02]

On a big IRS assessment, do not arouse the giant by calling yourself. Have a tax professional pull the transcripts and confirm the official statute date [Former IRS Agent Representation   4.2M Views — go3rRhIEajA @ 00:02:16]

sop_steps.title: Date-Stamp the Judgment and Revival Window
sop_steps.action: On receiving any revival summons, immediately compare the judgment date against the state revival or renewal deadline.
sop_steps.detail: Williams says that if a company comes at you with a revival summons, you need to look at it immediately, because a dormant judgment past the state window may not have to be paid [The Credit Repair Shop — 4Mctc4AuqWA @ 00:09:21]

sop_steps.title: Answer, Appear Early, and Master the Logistics
sop_steps.action: File the answer on time and scout the courthouse or Zoom setup before every hearing.
sop_steps.detail: Skiba has seen self-represented consumers drive to the courthouse the day before to learn parking, check-in, and security. They also won cases when the collector's attorney showed up late and the court threw the case out [Consumer Warrior — fWHpyqQu_5M @ 00:02:35]

sop_steps.title: Pull the Card Agreement and Compel Arbitration
sop_steps.action: Locate the arbitration clause, attach it to a motion to compel private arbitration, and then file with AAA in good faith.
sop_steps.detail: Skiba's motion attaches the clause and tells the judge that either party can request arbitration. If the court compels it, the creditor usually abandons the case [Consumer Warrior — 7TbwIGMYgYE @ 00:05:27]

sop_steps.title: Settle Low From a Position of Leverage
sop_steps.action: Make settlement offers below what you can actually pay, using the collector's cost of collection as pressure.
sop_steps.detail: Skiba says to start lower than the total you can pay because the collector always counters, and settlement talks are not admissible in court [Consumer Warrior — 7TbwIGMYgYE @ 00:07:39]. The Business Guy adds that the harder you are to collect from, the lower the settlement [The Business Guy | Asset Protection Planners — 5mmy9Xz_Oko @ 00:09:24]

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether time alone ever frees a debtor once a creditor holds a judgment. Steve Richardson of Richardson Law Offices, a southern New Jersey collection defense attorney, tells callers being levied on a ten-year-old judgment that once suit is brought and judgment is entered, the statute of limitations no longer applies and the clock stops ticking [wibZgw9EKZ4 @ 00:00:27]. Weston Legal backs the filing-date rule and kills the process-server dodge: the clock stops when the lawsuit is filed, not when you are served, and a judgment can last 20 years in many states [HD3idZhyATA @ 00:00:48]. Stephen A Williams of The Credit Repair Shop runs the counter-playbook, conceding a 20-year maximum for a civil judgment but arguing that every state has a dormancy mechanism, and a collector who misses the revival window cannot renew; one Ohio caller faced a revival attempt 12 years into a 10-year revival window, two years past the deadline [--FOsBTlu2E @ 00:04:17]. The Business Guy reads the same map from the creditor side: California runs 10 years plus a 10-year renewal for a total of 20, while an Oklahoma judgment expires in five years but can be renewed every five years indefinitely, so a judgment can sit against a debtor for life [nbtlIEi4we0 @ 00:02:28].

State numbers conflict between practitioners, which is why both Williams and Alex Carillo push viewers to check their own state before acting. Williams reads Illinois as a seven-year revival window and Georgia as seven years [4Mctc4AuqWA @ 00:03:39], while Carillo of Gustan Cho Associates has heard Illinois runs 20 years and Georgia seven, openly calling those figures guesses and telling viewers to look up the judgment rules where they live [SvBZyaCOSrc @ 00:01:05]. On federal tax debt the split is tactical rather than numerical. Former IRS agent Mike Sullivan warns that the IRS can extend the 10-year collection clock, or the taxpayer may have extended it already, through a bankruptcy, an offer in compromise, an appeals filing, a CDP filing, a lawsuit, time out of the country, or a signed waiver [go3rRhIEajA @ 00:01:38]. In a later video Sullivan flatly states the IRS just doesn't extend it on its own, and that only some action by the taxpayer extends the statute [0jHEJqFcgLA @ 00:02:56]. Enrolled agent Bob Jablonsky turns the clock into a timing weapon: an offer in compromise can be the best alternative right after assessment, but nine years and ten months in, the smarter play is to skip the offer and let the clock expire [KU5hNE5Z2MU @ 00:04:54].

The defensive playbooks split along wealth lines. The Business Guy pushes an offshore asset protection trust, typically a Cook Islands trust holding an LLC with the firm acting as trustee, because U.S. courts lack jurisdiction over the foreign trustee, and calls bankruptcy almost always a mistake for anyone with significant assets, since Chapter 7 strips non-exempt assets and a bankruptcy trustee's collection tools are ruthless [5mmy9Xz_Oko @ 00:10:04]. John Skiba of Consumer Warrior, with 23 years and over 400 debt collection trials, treats bankruptcy as the nuclear option that stops lawsuits, garnishments, and collections immediately and typically wraps a Chapter 7 in four to five months [fWHpyqQu_5M @ 00:13:15]. On negotiation, The Business Guy says leverage comes from making collection expensive because lawyers love low-hanging fruit, while Consumer Warrior counts settling a $5,000 suit for $800 or $1,000 as a clean win worth chasing before trial [7TbwIGMYgYE @ 00:06:56]. Fight Employment Discrimination adds a courtroom alternative from the EEOC side: an opponent's summary judgment motion forces them to tip their hand and show their evidence, and the counter is poking holes in their interpretation of the undisputed facts with your own documents, because neither the judge nor your own attorney will know your file the way you do [X9i8o5iRl9M @ 00:01:36].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failure is simply not showing up. Skiba says about 95% of people sued by a debt collector never file an answer, and without one the game is over: judgment, then wage garnishment or a bank levy, and with 70% of the country living paycheck to paycheck, losing a quarter of a check turns into a disaster fast [fWHpyqQu_5M @ 00:01:35]. Williams sees the same trap in revival court, where debt collection companies buy old judgments from original creditors and other collectors, and if the debtor does not show up there is no challenge, so the judgment gets renewed to finish out the 20 years, even in cases where it could not legally have been renewed [4Mctc4AuqWA @ 00:10:05]. Ducking service does not rescue anyone either; Weston Legal says people who plan to avoid the process server until the statute of limitations runs are wrong, because the clock is measured from filing, not service [HD3idZhyATA @ 00:00:34]. The same rule cuts in the debtor's favor: Skiba has won cases by arriving early to trials where the collector's attorney showed up late and the court threw the case out, because courts handling this volume run tight ships [fWHpyqQu_5M @ 00:02:11].

Sovereign-citizen theatrics fail fast. In a Travis County eviction captured by verdict sentencestv, Jose Martinez and Nicole Lewis entered a special appearance to challenge jurisdiction and announced they do not participate in legal contract; the judge pulled the address up on a map, found both personal and subject matter jurisdiction, and entered judgment for the landlord at $2,342.40 after neither tenant could say whether October or November rent had been paid [HPD6TM130zk @ 00:08:58]. Their VAWA argument was ruled no defense to nonpayment, the judge told them the judgment becomes final on day six absent action, and their answer was that they do not accept or consent to the orders [HPD6TM130zk @ 00:10:23]. Juris Wire shows the criminal-court version: a self-represented defendant facing three driving-suspended files skipped a final pretrial, triggering three bench warrants, and the court had to call off 30 to 50 jurors along with the prosecution's witnesses [xCHuZoPk7vA @ 00:02:31]. Notices had gone to an old Kalamazoo address the defendant never updated, the claim of being an American national to whom Michigan rules do not apply went nowhere, and the judge sent the defendant to county jail on a $3,000 bond per file [xCHuZoPk7vA @ 00:07:00].

Testimony and structure traps finish off debtors who did show up. John Watson of Alabama Consumer Protection Lawyers, drawing on 25 years of trial work and roughly a thousand debt buyer cases, has never seen a client who actually knew whether the debt buyer bought the debt, so answering yes when asked to agree you owe my client simply loses the case; without the purchase agreement the buyer is not even in the ball game [xF2ZuR2-O4o @ 00:04:31]. Watson proves the volunteering trap from the winning side: an insurance executive, unprompted, admitted that agents who missed quota lost their health insurance, and that one volunteered answer fed a six-figure case [xF2ZuR2-O4o @ 00:18:33]. The Business Guy reports tenancy by the entirety protection evaporating on death or divorce; one man got a police visit about his wife's fatal accident and, the same day, an attorney ordering seizure of the former T by E assets [5mmy9Xz_Oko @ 00:08:37]. On tax debt, Jablonsky warns that repeatedly filing offers in compromise the IRS will never accept buys the taxpayer nothing, because every one of those filings extends the time the IRS has to collect [KU5hNE5Z2MU @ 00:05:31].

callout.title: Pre-Move Checks Before Touching an Old Judgment or Tax Clock
callout.body: Every loss reported here traces back to a missed appearance, an unverified clock, or an unforced admission. Clear these four checks before making any move on a judgment, revival notice, or IRS balance.
items: Calendar every answer deadline and hearing and arrive early; a missed answer ends the case, and courts handling this volume run tight ships [Consumer Warrior — fWHpyqQu_5M @ 00:02:11].

On any revival notice, check the state revival window against the original judgment date before the hearing; one Ohio collector filed two years past a 10-year window [The Credit Repair Shop — --FOsBTlu2E @ 00:04:17].
Never agree on the stand that you owe the debt buyer without personal knowledge of the purchase agreement; a yes loses the case [Alabama Consumer Protection Lawyers — xF2ZuR2-O4o @ 00:04:31].

Pull the IRS account transcript before filing an offer, appeal, CDP hearing, or bankruptcy, since each one extends the collection clock [Former IRS Agent Representation   4.2M Views — 0jHEJqFcgLA @ 00:01:21].

chapters.pull_quote: Once suit is brought and especially once judgment is entered, then the statute of limitations no longer applies. — Richardson Law Offices (wibZgw9EKZ4 @ 00:00:27).
action_checklist: On any revival summons, research whether the collector is still inside the state revival window before deciding to fight or settle [The Credit Repair Shop — --FOsBTlu2E @ 00:13:18].
File the answer on time and show up a few minutes early, in person or on Zoom, so the collector cannot win by default [Consumer Warrior — fWHpyqQu_5M @ 00:14:19].
If the collector sued after the limitations period expired, file a motion to dismiss laying out the deadline and the violation, and look at FDCPA exposure [Consumer Warrior — 7TbwIGMYgYE @ 00:02:40].
Pull the card agreement, find the arbitration clause, and move to compel arbitration with AAA, where the creditor fronts $2,500 to $5,000 [Consumer Warrior — fWHpyqQu_5M @ 00:07:45].

Pull IRS account transcripts to confirm the statute date, then request the self-releasing lien release from the Cincinnati service center by fax [Former IRS Agent Representation   4.2M Views — 0jHEJqFcgLA @ 00:03:33].
At trial, bring organized manila folders with copies for the judge and the lawyer, and never guess at an answer [Alabama Consumer Protection Lawyers — xF2ZuR2-O4o @ 00:28:19].
